title: Barriers 2025 — Part A
source: WSU Y5 Barriers 2025 MCQ, student reconstruction; stems rewritten, tested point preserved

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man reports two weeks of exertional breathlessness and chest discomfort. A fortnight earlier he had a sore throat and fever. He is now afebrile; JVP is raised, there is a soft apical systolic murmur and an added sound after S2.
questions.lead: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Post-viral heart failure in a young adult — raised JVP, functional MR from a dilated ventricle and an S3 — is myocarditis. Pericarditis gives a rub and positional pain, not failure; endocarditis needs fever and a source.
questions.point: Myocarditis presents as new heart failure (raised JVP, S3, functional MR) in a young person a fortnight after a viral illness.

questions.stem: A man on rosuvastatin for hypercholesterolaemia was given roxithromycin three days ago for a chest infection. He now has diffuse muscle aches. CK is 3000 U/L (RR 40–300).
questions.lead: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A macrolide added to a statin raises statin levels and precipitates myositis; the timing to the new drug is the clue. Polymyositis is subacute and proximal, not a 3-day story.
questions.point: Macrolides (roxithromycin, clarithromycin, erythromycin) added to a statin precipitate statin myositis — a raised CK days after the new script is drug interaction, not viral myositis.

questions.stem: A patient with shoulder pain has a positive lift-off (Gerber's) test — unable to lift the dorsum of the hand off the lumbar spine.
questions.lead: Which muscle is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: Lift-off isolates internal rotation, which is subscapularis. Empty-can tests supraspinatus; resisted external rotation tests infraspinatus/teres minor.
questions.point: Gerber's lift-off test isolates subscapularis (internal rotation); empty-can is supraspinatus, resisted external rotation is infraspinatus/teres minor.

questions.stem: A man has right shoulder pain on abduction. Abduction is painless to 45°, painful from 45° to 135°, then painless again above 135°.
questions.lead: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Rupture of the long head of biceps
questions.explanation: A painful arc between roughly 60° and 120° is subacromial impingement of the rotator cuff. Frozen shoulder restricts all movements, particularly external rotation; ACJ pain is at the top of the arc (>170°).
questions.point: A painful arc of abduction (~60–120°) with pain-free extremes is rotator cuff impingement; a high painful arc >170° points to the ACJ, and global restriction to adhesive capsulitis.

questions.stem: A 3-day-old term infant is brought in with bilious vomiting and has not passed meconium since birth.
questions.lead: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Failure to pass meconium in 48 hours plus bilious vomiting is Hirschsprung until proven otherwise. Duodenal atresia vomits within hours of birth and meconium may pass; NEC is a preterm disease; pyloric stenosis is non-bilious at 3–6 weeks.
questions.point: No meconium by 48 hours plus bilious vomiting in a term neonate is Hirschsprung disease; duodenal atresia vomits within hours and pyloric stenosis is non-bilious at 3–6 weeks.

questions.stem: A woman in preterm labour at 31 weeks receives two doses of betamethasone. Hours after delivery the neonate develops subcostal recession and nasal flaring.
questions.lead: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: At 31 weeks surfactant deficiency dominates; steroids reduce but do not abolish RDS. TTN is a term/near-term, often caesarean, phenomenon; meconium aspiration is a term or post-term problem.
questions.point: Respiratory distress in a 31-week neonate is surfactant-deficiency RDS even after antenatal steroids; TTN belongs to term babies and meconium aspiration to term/post-term.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman with bipolar disorder and hypertension has a week of confusion, nausea, vomiting and thirst. She takes amlodipine, hydrochlorothiazide, lisinopril, lithium SR and sertraline. She is afebrile with a normal urine dipstick, a coarse action tremor and bilateral finger-nose ataxia; MMSE 24/30.
questions.lead: What is the most likely cause of her confusion?
questions.explanation: Tremor, ataxia, GI upset and confusion on lithium — with a thiazide and an ACE inhibitor both reducing lithium clearance — is toxicity. Normal dipstick and afebrile argue against UTI; dementia does not arrive over a week.
questions.point: Lithium toxicity presents with coarse tremor, ataxia, GI upset and confusion, and is precipitated by thiazides, ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs and dehydration.

questions.stem: A young man presents after taking an unknown drug. Pupils are constricted and respiratory rate is 6/min.
questions.lead: What is the most likely substance?
questions.explanation: Pinpoint pupils with respiratory depression is the opioid toxidrome. Benzodiazepines sedate but do not usually cause miosis or such profound respiratory depression alone.
questions.point: Miosis plus respiratory depression is the opioid toxidrome — treat with naloxone; benzodiazepines alone rarely drop the respiratory rate this far.

questions.stem: Which set of observations meets the definition of septic shock, assuming a suspected infective source in each?
questions.lead: Choose the best fit.
questions.explanation: Septic shock is sepsis with persisting hypotension needing vasopressors to hold MAP ≥65 (and lactate >2) after fluid. Hypothermia is a sepsis criterion too — fever is not required. Only option C is hypotensive.
questions.point: Septic shock = sepsis plus hypotension persisting after fluids (vasopressors to keep MAP ≥65, lactate >2 mmol/L); hypothermia counts, and fever is not required.

questions.stem: A toddler still on a milk-predominant diet with little solid food is tired and pale. Hb is low with low MCV and MCH; film shows hypochromic microcytic cells with anisocytosis.
questions.lead: What is the next investigation?
questions.explanation: Microcytic hypochromic anaemia in a milk-fed toddler is dietary iron deficiency — confirm with ferritin/iron studies before anything else. Electrophoresis is for thalassaemia once iron deficiency is excluded.
questions.point: Microcytic hypochromic anaemia in a milk-heavy toddler is iron deficiency: iron studies first, electrophoresis only after iron deficiency is excluded.

questions.stem: On routine bloods an otherwise well adult has a mildly raised bilirubin with completely normal ALT, ALP and GGT.
questions.lead: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with a normal remaining LFT panel in a well person is Gilbert's — a benign UGT1A1 defect, worse with fasting and illness. Haemolysis would show a raised retic count and LDH.
questions.point: Isolated mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with otherwise normal LFTs in a well adult is Gilbert syndrome; check a reticulocyte count only if haemolysis is a concern.

questions.stem: Regarding testicular tumours, which statement is TRUE?
questions.lead: Choose one.
options: They are the 6th most common malignancy in young men
Peak incidence of teratoma is at 70 years
Only 15% of stage 1 teratomas are cured by orchidectomy alone
Chemotherapy has no role in metastatic disease
questions.explanation: Seminomas are exquisitely radiosensitive (and chemosensitive). Testicular cancer is the commonest solid tumour in young men; teratomas peak in the 20s; stage 1 disease is cured by orchidectomy in the large majority; metastatic disease is highly curable with cisplatin-based chemotherapy.
questions.point: Seminomas are radiosensitive; testicular cancer is the commonest solid malignancy of young men, and even metastatic disease is usually cured with platinum chemotherapy.

questions.stem: A man with heart failure takes an ACE inhibitor, spironolactone, a beta blocker and frusemide, and develops gynaecomastia.
questions.lead: Which drug is responsible?
questions.explanation: Spironolactone is an anti-androgen at the receptor. Eplerenone is the switch if it matters.
questions.point: Spironolactone causes gynaecomastia through anti-androgen activity; eplerenone is the alternative mineralocorticoid antagonist without that effect.

questions.stem: A woman at 37 weeks has 50 mL of painless bright vaginal bleeding. She is not in labour and the uterus is soft.
questions.lead: What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Painless third-trimester bleeding with a soft uterus is praevia; abruption is painful with a tense, tender uterus. Show is mucous and small-volume. Do not perform a digital vaginal examination until praevia is excluded on ultrasound.
questions.point: Painless bright APH with a soft uterus is placenta praevia (no digital VE until placental site is known); painful bleeding with a woody uterus is abruption.

questions.stem: Which statement about carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is TRUE?
questions.lead: Choose one.
options: The reference range depends on age
CEA can be raised in smokers
It is specific for colorectal cancer
It is specific for pancreatic cancer
It is a screening test for bowel cancer
questions.explanation: CEA is non-specific — raised in smokers, IBD, cirrhosis and several other cancers. Its use is monitoring for recurrence after colorectal resection, never screening.
questions.point: CEA is a monitoring marker for colorectal cancer recurrence, not a screening or diagnostic test — it is raised in smokers, IBD, cirrhosis and other malignancies.

questions.stem: An elderly woman with pelvic pathology involving the obturator foramen is suspected of having obturator nerve compression.
questions.lead: Where would you expect sensory change?
questions.explanation: The obturator nerve (L2–4) supplies the adductors and a patch of skin over the medial thigh. Lateral thigh is the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve; medial leg is the saphenous branch of the femoral nerve.
questions.point: Obturator nerve compression gives medial thigh sensory loss and weak adduction; lateral thigh numbness is meralgia paraesthetica (lateral femoral cutaneous), medial leg is saphenous.

questions.stem: Which lymph nodes are the primary drainage of a testicular tumour and must be assessed at staging?
questions.lead: Choose one.
questions.explanation: The testis descends from the posterior abdominal wall and keeps its para-aortic lymphatic drainage. The scrotal skin drains to the inguinal nodes — which is why trans-scrotal biopsy is forbidden.
questions.point: Testicular tumours drain to the para-aortic nodes (embryological origin), which is why staging is by CT abdomen and why trans-scrotal biopsy — which would seed inguinal nodes — is never done.

questions.stem: A man has occlusive atherosclerosis at the aortic bifurcation.
questions.lead: Which symptom is most characteristic?
options: Paraesthesia of the dorsum of the foot
questions.explanation: Aortoiliac disease (Leriche syndrome) gives buttock and thigh claudication with erectile dysfunction and absent femoral pulses. Calf claudication is femoropopliteal disease.
questions.point: Aortoiliac (Leriche) disease = bilateral buttock/thigh claudication, erectile dysfunction and absent femoral pulses; calf claudication localises to the superficial femoral artery.

questions.stem: Which organism has essentially never developed resistance to penicillin?
questions.lead: Choose one.
questions.explanation: Group A strep remains universally penicillin-sensitive, which is why penicillin is still first-line for pharyngitis, cellulitis and rheumatic fever prophylaxis. Staphylococci, E. coli and gonococcus are all commonly resistant.
questions.point: Streptococcus pyogenes has never acquired penicillin resistance — penicillin remains first-line for GAS pharyngitis, cellulitis and rheumatic fever prophylaxis.

questions.stem: Which piece of information is NOT used in the TNM staging of colorectal carcinoma?
questions.lead: Choose one.
questions.explanation: Colorectal T-stage is depth of invasion through the bowel wall, not size. Size matters in breast and renal staging, which is the trap.
questions.point: Colorectal cancer T-stage is depth of wall invasion, not tumour size — size drives T-stage in breast and kidney, not bowel.
